This is a pretty good puzzle-ish game all things considered, but I put this as recommended only on the condition that this game is on sale for $5 or less. The game introduces new quirks and puzzle elements at a steady pace, and there are certain points where you need to apply everything you learned and think outside the box to progress - the feeling you get after figuring it out is really satisfying. The problem is that even though you're given new things to play with, in the end it's all the same. You're given four different exe files gradually that can render a security system vulnerable, but you simply type their filenames and execute them. That's what most of the game is, typing the same things over and over again. Some text files you find in the victims' computers are amusing and some emails are funny, but that's as diverse as it gets.

Pick it up if you want some fun for two hours or so, but this is definitely not a game I'd value at $10. The only reason I got it was because Steam had a weekend where you can keep the game permanently if you simply downloaded it.

In [i]Hacknet[/i], you play as a computer user who has just been bestowed a unique operating system (OS) with tools that can hack different computers. As the game progresses, you will discover new hacking tools, join other factions of hackers, fulfill hacking job contracts to build your reputation, and solve the game’s central mystery.

What I love about [i]Hacknet[/i] is the high level of immersion and engaging pacing. With my headphones on, listening to the adrenaline-pumping soundtrack, I voraciously took on one hacking contract after another. Before long, two to three hours have flown by. The game's missions, though all require hacking, vary in objects and pacing. Because of that, I did not find gameplay repetitive, and I used every opportunity to familiarize myself with the tools I had at my disposal. All of this prepared me for the climatic final mission, which totally did not disappoint.

[i]Hacknet[/i] is novice-friendly, but some players may find it having a slightly steep learning curve. Players will be at an advantage if they can type fast, has used *nix (e.g. Linux) shell commands, and/or are familiar with text-based OSes. This is because the user interface of [i]Hacknet[/i] is austere, with typing as your primary form of input. Still, there are simple graphics to depict hacking progress, network of computers, and directory trees. You can use your mouse from time to time as means of in-game navigation as I did.

[i]Hacknet[/i]'s appeal aside from immersion and pacing is really its simplicity. The players will always be given all the tools they would need to complete missions. So, the real challenge is to figure out which tool(s) to use to hack the computers and phones, and to do it quickly and efficiently. So, think fast! Type fast and furious! Once the dust has settled, snooping around the hacked machines and reaping your rewards are gratifying.

At the time of this review, [i]Hacknet[/i] is my favourite hacking-themed game. It’s fast, it’s empowering, and it’s extremely gratifying -- especially after a challenging mission. I highly recommend this game to those who wish an adrenaline-pumping, brain-teasing, text-based adventure game.

It all serves as a great base for what could be a killer game (or one of the best educational titles), had the devs decided to go further with the idea. At this point, the story is linear, although the topic screams for difficult moral choices. Being it a text-based game, story-shaping decisions could be expected but I didn't encouter any. I actually didn't finish this game, but I read a story synopsis and it was, well, not too creative. Decent, but not amazing. The reason I didn't finish is because the story effectively takes a break for about 8-10 hours after the first hour, having you invest into smaller stories that you come across in small missions. The other reason I didn't finish was that the gameplay felt like actual hacking and work, and it was the kind of grindy, difficult work that one might receive in a classroom. Some features of the UI were extremely difficult to operate, and while that was somewhat realistic, I came to play a game, not because I liked doing difficult computer work, which is part of the reason why some hackers become hackers. Speaking of that, this game makes hacking extremely easy and simplified. I guess that if a hacking OS was developed in real life, it may actually be this easy, but in reality now hacking is way more difficult, complicated and sometimes more fun than this.

The world building and details were fantastic. I can't tell you how many times I laughed scrolling through logs on PCs I'd hacked into. They were well written and funny. But the massive break from the story made me feel like I was actually doing hacker work (although way too easy) and not playing a game. I came to experience a story, play a game, be something and someone else for a while, not to actually do hacker work. This game did not advertise as a hacker sim, but as a game where you play as a hacker with a story. That is my main problem with this game.

And don't get me wrong--I am all about games that require you do think and reflect and do not have big visuals or explosions or gunfights--this game's gameplay was boring. I've already said how the hacking was too easy and the UI was way too hard, but simply, hacking got boring rather quickly. That's basically it. In terms of additional information, there were no bugs and it was programmed very solidly. 

Overall, get this game when it is very cheap and play it for a few hours. You can have more fun with it than just two hours, so you don't have to return it, just buy it very cheap or free, that's how I got this game, it was free for a limited time and I downloaded it. 79/100 -- good, just not a B.

Ever want to be a Hacker? or at least pretend ? Well in Hacknet, its an immersive hacking terminal based simulator. Trust me it looks and feels pretty legit. If it wasn't for the ambient music in the background, sometimes you do feel like your well, hacking.  Start with making a profile and then a tutorial, to learn the ins and the outs of how to get into someones computer then probe, scan and do whatever to the files as you want/need. Then from there, work on contracts or jobs to boost your reputation to gain entry into some pretty hardcore hacker groups like Entropy and CSEC. These open up harder contracts and jobs and progresses the story line of the game. The game bases on you learning and memorizing what to do as you go along to get faster. It's all about punching in the right programming codes into the terminal at the right time.  Yes, typing is the game. Some contracts and jobs are rather well written and clever, so reading is suggested while hacking other peoples computers. Some jobs seem like viable legit reasons why there are hackers. Not all the jobs are for nefarious reasons. Arch- Nemesis? WHY YES ,THERE IS ONE! It does great to the story line. I suggest that when you get hacked yourself, it may look very very real and if you have really immersed yourself into the game, you might freak and turn your computer off. Remember behind every spy and secret agent, there's that computer techie that knows his stuff and gets them through the day. That's you. The game is rather straight forward graphics of terminal, colored windows and ambient music. Not an action game. There is a fun lil clicker game, within the game you can hack into, if that's your thing.

I got Hacknet for free, but truth to be told, I should've bought this game if I knew about it. Amazing UI, gameplay, story, works great on modern PC, and not to mention the soundtrack is super amazing and cues in on the right moment. I'm planning to get the DLC later just to play more of this.

The terminal mode is very similar to Unix systems like Linux. I've used a lot of different Linux distros in the past and used terminal extensively, and I have to say, this is an amazing level of detail coming from an indie game. It's very close to the Unix experience and I found myself naturally using it a lot.

Every systems here have reference to the real world hacking (whereas other hacking games are purely fictional), its just that it is simplified to the point where you can just type a few letters to run the program (like a script kiddie). You can hack almost every systems in the game. Almost everything is also self-consistent too, even the HTML source can be edited.

I wanted to praise more about what this game did right, but I don't want to spoil anything, so I'll say just say that this game, gives you an environment where you feel like you are a true hacker, and you are surrounded by 4chan-style hacking community. And once you managed to hack the hardest thing ever, it gives you great satisfaction about it.

Hacknet also blends command line with puzzle very well, feels very similar to real world hacking.

My only complain was that it was too short and I wished that there is more functionality in the command line and your OS to create new folders etc, but I guess it was ok for a game that's just about simulating hacking and not simulating everything.

Also, I've got 100% achievement on this game. I rarely do achievement for any games, but this game is worth doing the achievements as you learn more about this game.

Overall, this is the best script kiddie simulator that I've played thus far and you should definitely buy this game, 9/10.

There are plenty of good programming games out there, but I've been looking for a hacking game for a while, and I've finally found it with Hacknet. It offers a good balance of realism with use of the command line needed to use hacking tools and navigate through computers, with the fun of being a computer whiz, with cool visuals accompanying each tool.

The gameplay consists of breaking some number of ports, then using those ports to hack into the computer. From there, you'll accomplish some mission set out for you, which can range in difficulty from finding and deleting a file, to hacking multiple computers in a network to complete a complex task. While this may not sound that hard, some computers have time limits for hacking, which makes it even more tense, and very satisfying when you break in just a second or two before time's up. In addition, while some of the beginning tasks are relatively easy, there are some very good story missions, including having to hunt for clues by looking at files, and there is at least 1 mission that will have you questioning your morals.

I had a ton of fun with the game, and I would highly recommend it to anybody looking for a hacking/programming game.

This game is so enticing in a way I can't put my finger on.  I know nothing about coding and never had an interest in it, so I can't explain why this game drew me in the way it did. Several of the missions force you into ethical dilemmas, including potentially lethal ones, which add an extra bit of tension to already tense situations.  The music is also a driving force in the game and becomes very intense during difficult hacks.  I originally thought I would turn the music off and just listen to my own, but I found myself enjoying it too much to get rid of it.  

I just finished a 3-day binge of this game (including the DLC: Labyrinths which could easily be called Hacknet 2 with all the content it includes).  I played it through twice; the first time I ended up playing and finishing the DLC without realizing it (Kaguya Trials FYI), so I went back and played it again to finish the original story line.  

I have had so much fun playing this game, and I plan to play it again as there are still missions I want to complete including another, more aggressive, pathway to venture down.  I would highly recommend this game.
